actions.name: Mental status examination
actions.result: Alert, cooperative, well-groomed. Speech normal rate/rhythm/volume. Mood 'okay I guess.' Affect mildly restricted but reactive. Thought process linear, goal-directed. No SI/HI/AVH. Insight fair, judgment intact. Cognition grossly intact.

actions.name: Suicide/homicide risk assessment
actions.result: Denies current or recent suicidal ideation, intent, or plan. Denies homicidal ideation. No access-to-firearms concern reported. No prior suicide attempts. Protective factors: job, family, future orientation.

actions.name: Mania/hypomania screen (current symptoms)
actions.result: Denies elevated/irritable mood, decreased need for sleep, grandiosity, racing thoughts, impulsivity, or increased goal-directed activity over past 2 weeks. Sleeping about 7 hours nightly.

actions.name: Depression screen (current symptoms)
actions.result: Denies anhedonia, hopelessness, guilt, or psychomotor changes. Describes mood as flat/subdued rather than sad. Appetite stable.

actions.name: Camera-guided tremor assessment (outstretched hands)
actions.result: Patient holds both arms outstretched on camera; visible moderate-amplitude postural tremor of both hands, worse on action (reaching for cup). No asterixis noted. No ataxia or dysarthria observed on brief exam.

actions.name: Camera-guided gait and coordination check
actions.result: Patient walks a few steps in frame and performs finger-to-nose bilaterally; gait steady, finger-to-nose intact, no dysmetria.

actions.name: Home/clinic vitals review
actions.result: BP 122/78 mmHg, HR 88 bpm, Temp 37.1°C, Weight 86 kg (stable). No orthostatic symptoms reported.

actions.name: Review today's lithium level
actions.result: Lithium 1.4 mmol/L (therapeutic range 0.6-1.2 mmol/L) — H, drawn ~12 hours post-dose per patient report (standard trough timing); prior levels in the flowsheet were drawn at routine follow-up visits but timing relative to last dose was not documented, so comparability to today's properly-timed trough level is uncertain.

actions.name: Review renal function panel
actions.result: Creatinine 1.3 mg/dL (H, baseline 0.9 mg/dL three months ago); eGFR 68 mL/min/1.73m² (L); BUN 22 mg/dL (H). This represents a significant creatinine rise (ratio 1.3/0.9 = 1.44) concerning for lithium-related renal impairment, but it does not meet strict KDIGO AKI criteria at all: KDIGO requires a rise of ≥0.3 mg/dL within 48 hours or a 1.5-1.9x rise from baseline within 7 days, and this change occurred over 3 months with no interim creatinine data. Best characterized as a significant creatinine rise of uncertain acuity, warranting urgent medical work-up rather than labeled 'AKI.'

actions.name: Review thyroid function (TSH)
actions.result: TSH 5.8 mIU/L (H, reference 0.4-4.5 mIU/L); free T4 pending/not yet drawn this visit.

actions.name: Review electrolyte panel
actions.result: Sodium 143 mEq/L (H end of normal), Potassium 4.1 mEq/L, Chloride 104 mEq/L, Bicarbonate 23 mEq/L — mild hemoconcentration pattern consistent with volume depletion.

actions.name: Review pharmacy fill/refill history
actions.result: Lithium carbonate 300 mg capsules, #90 every 30 days, last filled on schedule — adherence by refill timing appears consistent. Ibuprofen 600 mg tablets started 3 weeks ago, OTC/prescribed by urgent care, no interaction warning flagged in pharmacy system (NSAID-lithium interaction not systematically screened).

actions.name: Review prior psychiatric note (14 months ago, lithium initiation)
actions.result: Diagnosis bipolar I disorder confirmed after manic episode with psychotic features requiring hospitalization. Lithium carbonate initiated and titrated to 900 mg nightly with good response. Baseline labs at that time: Cr 0.8 mg/dL, TSH 2.1 mIU/L, lithium level 0.7 mmol/L.

actions.name: Columbia Suicide Severity Rating Scale (C-SSRS) screen
actions.result: Negative for current ideation, intent, plan, or lifetime attempts.

actions.name: Review home fluid intake/urination log (patient-reported)
actions.result: Patient estimates drinking 10-12 glasses of water/day and urinating 'every hour,' with 2-3 loose bowel movements daily for 2 weeks.

actions.name: Review EKG from lithium initiation workup (baseline)
actions.result: Sinus rhythm, rate 72, normal intervals, no abnormalities. No repeat EKG performed today.

mismatches.patientClaim: Patient reports taking lithium 900 mg nightly as prescribed and rarely missing doses.
mismatches.recordEvidence: Pharmacy refill history shows lithium refilled consistently every ~30 days for 14 months with no gaps, which actually supports adherence rather than contradicting it — the real issue is that the pharmacy system did NOT flag the NSAID-lithium interaction when ibuprofen was dispensed, despite his established lithium regimen being on file.
mismatches.teachingPoint: Adherence can be confirmed objectively via refill history, redirecting attention to the real driver of toxicity (NSAID interaction plus volume depletion) rather than nonadherence — and highlights a systems gap in medication interaction screening across prescribers.

mismatches.patientClaim: Patient says his back pain is much better since starting ibuprofen and does not connect it to his current symptoms.
mismatches.recordEvidence: Medication list confirms ibuprofen 600 mg TID started 3 weeks ago, overlapping exactly with the 2-week onset of polyuria, polydipsia, tremor, and diarrhea plus the renal function decline and lithium elevation shown in the lab trend.
mismatches.teachingPoint: Patients may not spontaneously link a seemingly unrelated new medication (treating an unrelated problem) to new systemic symptoms; the clinician must actively connect medication timing to the toxicity presentation rather than relying on the patient to flag it.

objectives.text: Recognize signs and symptoms of lithium toxicity (tremor, GI symptoms, polyuria/polydipsia) in the context of a rising lithium level and acute kidney injury.
Identify NSAID co-administration and volume depletion (hot kitchen, double shifts, GI losses) as precipitants of acute lithium toxicity and renal impairment.
Perform a thorough current-episode mood and risk assessment to confirm euthymia and rule out acute mania, depression, or suicidality despite medication nonadherence concerns.

Through nonjudgmental, direct interview questioning and rapport-building (not surfaced by a generic MSE), elicit the patient's hidden ambivalence about lithium and covert consideration of self-discontinuation, and address it therapeutically.

Interpret trended lithium, renal, and thyroid labs to distinguish acute toxicity from chronic nephrogenic/thyroid effects, and use pharmacy refill records to assess true adherence versus an interaction-driven toxicity.

Formulate an appropriate, in-scope management plan: hold or reduce lithium, ensure urgent medical/renal evaluation for toxicity and AKI, discontinue the offending NSAID, arrange close lab follow-up, and address thyroid dysfunction with primary care referral rather than independently managing acute toxicity.

answerKey.primaryProblem: Acute lithium toxicity (serum lithium 1.4 mmol/L, up from 0.8 three months ago) with a significant creatinine rise (1.3 mg/dL vs. baseline 0.9 mg/dL three months ago) concerning for lithium-induced renal impairment — this does not meet strict KDIGO AKI criteria (which require a defined rise within 48 hours to 7 days), as the change occurred over 3 months with no interim labs — precipitated by NSAID (ibuprofen) use combined with volume depletion from heat exposure and GI losses, in a patient with bipolar I disorder currently euthymic on long-term lithium maintenance.
differential: Acute lithium toxicity due to NSAID interaction and dehydration (most likely)
Lithium-induced nephrogenic diabetes insipidus (chronic, contributing to polyuria/polydipsia independent of acute toxicity)
Subclinical hypothyroidism, possibly lithium-induced, contributing to fatigue but not the acute presentation

Significant creatinine rise from another cause (e.g., prerenal azotemia from volume depletion) amplifying lithium retention; does not meet KDIGO AKI timing criteria given the 3-month interval between the two available creatinine values and lack of interim data
Early breakthrough mania or mixed episode (unlikely given MSE and screens, but must be ruled out given tremor and GI symptoms)
Thyrotoxicosis (unlikely; TSH is elevated, not suppressed)
Nonadherence leading to erratic lithium dosing (ruled out by refill history)
keyFindings: Lithium level 1.4 mmol/L today, up from 0.8 mmol/L three months ago, now above therapeutic range (0.6-1.2)

Creatinine 1.3 mg/dL (up from baseline 0.9), eGFR 68 (L), BUN 22 (H) — a significant rise concerning for lithium-induced renal impairment, but does NOT meet KDIGO AKI criteria since the only two data points span 3 months with no interim creatinine, far outside the 48-hour/7-day window KDIGO requires
New-onset worsened postural/action tremor on camera exam, beyond baseline mild tremor
2-week history of polydipsia, polyuria, and loose stools consistent with lithium GI/renal toxicity and nephrogenic diabetes insipidus
Ibuprofen 600 mg TID started 3 weeks ago (NSAID reduces renal lithium clearance), overlapping precisely with symptom onset
Volume depletion risk factors: hot kitchen, double shifts, heavy sweating, diarrhea
TSH 5.8 mIU/L (H), subclinical hypothyroidism, a known long-term lithium effect requiring primary care follow-up
Pharmacy refill history confirms adherence, ruling out erratic dosing as the cause
Current mood euthymic; MSE and mania/depression screens negative; C-SSRS negative

Hidden ambivalence: patient privately misses hypomanic energy and has been considering stopping lithium independently, not yet acted upon — only elicitable through direct, nonjudgmental interview questioning, not through the MSE itself
plan: Advise patient to hold tonight's lithium dose and seek urgent same-day medical evaluation (primary care or emergency department) given the significant creatinine rise and lithium level 1.4 mmol/L — this requires physical exam, IV fluids, and lab monitoring beyond psychiatry's remote scope
Instruct patient to stop ibuprofen immediately; coordinate with urgent care/primary care for alternative non-NSAID pain management for back strain

Recommend repeat lithium level and renal panel in 24-48 hours after rehydration, coordinated with primary care, before resuming or adjusting lithium dose, which will also help clarify the trajectory of the renal picture
Counsel on maintaining adequate hydration and avoiding future NSAID use without checking with the prescribing psychiatrist
Refer to primary care for evaluation and management of elevated TSH (consider repeat TSH with free T4 off acute illness, discuss levothyroxine if persistent)

Explore and validate the patient's ambivalence about lithium and sense of flatness/missing hypomanic energy, using direct nonjudgmental questioning during the interview rather than relying on the MSE alone; psychoeducate on relapse risk of stopping lithium abruptly and the difference between toxicity (temporary, treatable) and the medication itself being wrong for him

Schedule close psychiatric follow-up (within 1 week) after acute toxicity resolves to reassess lithium dosing, consider adjunctive strategies for residual flatness, and discuss long-term lithium monitoring plan (levels, renal, thyroid every 3-6 months, with consistent post-dose timing documented)
Document clear safety plan: no current SI/HI, but monitor given ambivalence about treatment and risk of mood destabilization if lithium is self-discontinued
Do not independently manage the acute toxicity/renal impairment as psychiatry; ensure a medical clinician is involved urgently
redFlags: Lithium level significantly above therapeutic range with new tremor and GI/renal symptoms indicating possible evolving toxicity, which can progress to confusion, ataxia, seizures, or arrhythmia if untreated
Significant creatinine rise (falling eGFR) requiring urgent medical, not purely psychiatric, management, even though it does not meet strict KDIGO AKI timing criteria
Patient's covert consideration of self-discontinuing lithium, which carries high relapse risk for mania given prior psychotic manic episode
Need to distinguish toxicity tremor/GI symptoms from any emerging mood episode before attributing symptoms solely to toxicity
educationPoints: NSAIDs (including OTC ibuprofen) significantly reduce renal clearance of lithium and are a common, under-recognized cause of lithium toxicity; cross-prescriber communication and pharmacy interaction screening are essential
Lithium toxicity can present subtly with worsening tremor, GI symptoms, and polyuria/polydipsia before progressing to neurologic signs like confusion or ataxia

Routine lithium monitoring (levels, renal function, thyroid function every 3-6 months) is essential even when patients feel clinically stable, since toxicity can develop insidiously; levels should ideally be drawn at a consistent, documented time post-dose (standard is ~12 hours) to allow valid comparison across visits
Patients on long-term mood stabilizers may privately grieve the loss of hypomanic energy; nonjudgmental, direct inquiry (not the MSE itself) can uncover covert nonadherence risk before it happens
Volume depletion from occupational heat exposure, poor fluid replacement physiology, and diarrhea can precipitate lithium toxicity even without any change in dose or adherence
Subclinical hypothyroidism is a known long-term adverse effect of lithium and requires ongoing primary care collaboration, not psychiatric management alone

KDIGO AKI criteria require a creatinine rise of ≥0.3 mg/dL within 48 hours, or a 1.5-1.9x rise from baseline within 7 days; a creatinine increase documented only before and after a much longer interval (here, 3 months, with no interim data) does not meet KDIGO AKI criteria at all, regardless of the magnitude of the ratio — a key nuance for trainees to avoid misapplying diagnostic criteria to real-world lab spacing

scenario.studentBrief: You are the psychiatry resident conducting a telehealth medication management follow-up for Gabriel Costa, a 29-year-old sous-chef with bipolar I disorder stable on lithium carbonate 900 mg nightly for 14 months. He is calling in with concerns about worsening tremor, thirst, urination, and loose stools over the past 2 weeks. Review the chart, conduct the interview and mental status/risk assessment, and determine next steps.
scenario.chiefComplaint: Worsening hand tremor, excessive thirst and urination, and loose stools for 2 weeks in a patient on long-term lithium.
scenario.openingLine: Hey doc, thanks for fitting me in. My hands have been shaking a lot more lately, I'm super thirsty all the time, going to the bathroom constantly, and my stomach's been loose too. It's starting to mess with my work.
tasks: Take a focused history of the tremor, thirst, urination, and gastrointestinal symptoms
Review the medication list and recent changes with the patient
Conduct a mental status examination and assess risk
Review the laboratory results with the patient
Explore the patient's experience with and feelings about his current medication regimen
Formulate and agree a management plan with appropriate follow-up

profile.setting: Telehealth video visit, patient at home in Providence, Rhode Island, calling from his bedroom before an evening shift
profile.summary: A 29-year-old sous-chef with bipolar I disorder stable on lithium for 14 months presents to a telepsychiatry medication follow-up with two weeks of worsening tremor, polydipsia, polyuria, and diarrhea. The case teaches recognition of acute lithium toxicity precipitated by NSAID use and volume depletion, interpretation of trended labs, and nonjudgmental elicitation of covert ambivalence about mood-stabilizer treatment, while keeping management within psychiatry's telehealth scope by escalating the acute toxicity/AKI to urgent medical care.
profile.title: Worsening Tremor and Thirst in a Chef Stable on Lithium: Recognizing Acute Toxicity
